It is whether the declared type of an ANL is an approximate numeric type or the decimal floating-point type with an precision. If the declared type of ANL is an approximate numeric type, then the value of ANL shall not be greater than the maximum value nor less than the minimum value that can be represented by the approximate numeric types. If the declared type of ANL is the decimal floating-point type, then the value of ANL shall not be greater than the maximum value nor less than the minimum value that can be represented by the decimal floating-point type.
WG3:YYJ-102 = H2-2001-___ Thus the only syntax error for an is what is commonly known as overflow; there is no syntax error for specifying more significant digits than the SQL-implementation can represent internally, nor for specifying a value that has no exact equivalent in the SQL-implementations internal representation. (Underflow, specifying a non-zero value so close to 0 (zero) that the closest representation in the SQL-implementations internal representation is 0E0, is a special case of the latter condition, and is not a syntax error.)

The rows of the window partition are placed in window ordering groups, as follows: two rows are in the same window ordering group if and only if they are peers with regard to the , according to the General Rules of .
WG3:KMG-032 = DM32.2-2010-00089
Window ordering groups within a window partition are ordered as follows: window ordering group WOG1 precedes window ordering group WOG2 if some row R1 in WOG1 precedes some row R2 in WOG2 in the window ordering, according to the General Rules of .
WG3:KMG-032 = DM32.2-2010-00089 Since all rows in a window ordering group are peers with regard to the , if one row of WOG1 precedes one row of WOG2, then all rows of WOG1 precede all rows of WOG2.
WG3:KMG-032 = DM32.2-2010-00089 WG3:USN-024, P02-JPN-029
The distance between two window ordering groups WOG1 and WOG2 is number of window ordering groups between WOG1 and WOG2, inclusive, minus 1 (one).
WG3:KMG-032 = DM32.2-2010-00089 Thus the distance between a window ordering group WOG and itself is 1 (one) − 1 (one) = 0 (zero).
WG3:KMG-032 = DM32.2-2010-00089

A subset S of QNDG is strongly connected if either the cardinality of S is 1 (one) or there is a path from every node of S to every other node of S. A stratum is a maximal strongly connected subset of QNDG.
WG3:GLA-029 = DM32.2-2014-00008R2 A commonly used synonym for stratum is strongly connected component. Note that any cycle is strongly connected. If C1 and C2 are two strongly connected sets of nodes with non-empty intersection, then their union C1 C2 is also strongly connected. Hence, maximal strongly connected sets are found by forming unions of overlapping cycles. Every WQNi belongs to exactly one stratum; thus the set of strata forms a partitioning of QNDG.

WG3:CJU-018 = H2-2009-00126 In addition, by a Syntax Rule of , an operand of MAX or MIN must not be row-ordered. This is because the ordering of non-null row-ordered values is not a total ordering (for example, the relative order of the rows (1, null) and (null, 1) is indeterminate). The General Rules of , provide special rules to totally order rows containing null values, but these rules are not used in MAX or MIN. The other ordering operations do not require a total ordering.

WG3:W09-009, P02-NLD-017
Invoking an SQL-invoked routine
Execute the invocation of an SQL-invoked routine.
This Subclause is invoked by other Subclauses: call statement, prepare statement, cast specification, method invocation, and static method invocation.
The Syntax Rules of this Subclause are structured as though they constituted a subroutine that those other Subclause call; this "subroutine" defines three parameters: - a routine invocation - an SQL-path (optional) - a user-defined type (optional)
The Syntax Rules of this "subroutine" returns two results: - a subject routine - a static SQL argument list (I have not figured out whether this is always computed or not)
Invocation of the Syntax Rules of this Subclause requires that the invoking rules provide up to three arguments, corresponding to those three parameters. The routine invocation is always required. The SQL-path seems to be optional, as it is only supplied from method invocation and static method invocation; its purpose is to capture the SQL-path provided as part of a path-resolved user-defined type name or computed from a list of names of schemas containing a definition of some supertype of method invocation's user-defined type. The user-defined type is optional, as it only supplied from static method invocation; its purpose is to specify the required return type of the selected subject routine.
The Syntax Rules compute a subject routine from the information provided as arguments. It can (and seems to usually, but not always do) compute a static argument list from knowledge of the argument list in the original routine invocation and the selected subject routine. (I cannot prove yet that there are times when the static argument list is not computed, but I cannot yet prove that it always is.) The returns type is not returned when these Syntax Rules are invoked from call statement.

WG3:W16-043r1 deleted 1 Note
This Subclause is invoked by other Subclauses: call statement, prepare statement, cast specification, method invocation, and static method invocation.
The General Rules of this Subclause are structured as though they constituted a subroutine that those other Subclause call; this "subroutine" defines two parameters: - a subject routine - a static SQL argument list
This "subroutine" returns up to one result: - a value (but not when invoked from call statement)
Invocation of the General Rules of this Subclause requires that the invoking rules provide two arguments, corresponding to those two parameters. The subject routine is the routine that is invoked/executed by these General Rules. The static SQL argument list is used to compute a dynamic argument list that is provided to the routine as it is invoked.
Except when invoked from call statement (when these General Rules behave like a procedure invocation), these General Rules compute a value that represents the result of invoking the subject routine; in some cases, that value can be determined without invoking the subject routine (for example, when null values are provided as the value of certain arguments in the static SQL argument list).

XQuery regular expression matching
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
Determine a list of match vectors to an XQuery regular expression in a character string.
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2 Editorial to use SCsignature, symparam, and symreturn, 2006-09-27 Revise Subclause signature to document params/returns; Jim Melton, 2022-09-29
S PAT SP U FL
STRING — a character string within which a regular expression match is to be sought.
PATTERN — a character string that is an XQuery regular expression.
POSITION — an integer specifying the position within STRING at which the regular expression match operation is to start.
UNITS — an indication of whether the regular expression match is performed in units of characters (CHARACTERS) or in units of octets (OCTETS).
FLAG — a character string that is an XQuery option flag.
LIST — a list of match vectors, each of which is a pair of integers specifying the starting position and length of a regular expression match in STRING.
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
Case:
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2

WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2 WG3:SQL-050 = DM32.2-2011-00___

If P is not an XQuery regular expression, then an exception condition is raised: .

WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
Let LEN be the length in characters of S.
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
A position/length PL is a pair of exact numeric values, a position P and a length L, such that either P = 0 (zero) and L = 0 (zero), or P is positive, L is non-negative, and P + L LEN + 1 (one). If P is positive, then PL represents the substring of S whose starting position is P and whose length is L. If P is 0 (zero), then PL does not represent a substring of S.
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2 WG3:USN-024, P02-JPN-048 For example, if S is a, then there are four position/lengths, namely (1,0), denoting the zero-length substring at the beginning of S; (2,0), denoting the zero-length substring at the end of S; (1,1), denoting the whole string S; and (0,0), denoting no substring of S.
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
Let G be the number of parenthesized groups in PAT.
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2 WG3:UTC-013 P02-NLD-008
An XQuery regular expression match is defined as follows.
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
Case:
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
If the character repertoire of S is UCS, then an XQuery regular expression match is a match as defined by for the function fn:matches(), with F as the value of the parameter $flags, with the following modifications:
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
The metacharacters ^, $, and . are interpreted according to the guidelines of RL1.6 Line boundaries, in .
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
The multi-character escape \s matches 0020 (space), 0009 (tab), or any single character or two-character sequence identified as a newline sequence by RL1.6 line boundaries in .
WG3:KOA-024 = DM32.2-2011-00007
The multi-character escape \S matches any single character that is not matched by a single character that matches the multi-character escape \s.
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
Otherwise, the definition of XQuery regular expression match is .
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
A match vector MV is an array of G + 1 position/lengths, indexed from 0 (zero) through G. MV represents an XQuery regular expression match of PAT, including information about capture groups. MV[0] is the position/length that denotes the entire XQuery regular expression match of PAT. For i between 1 (one) and G, MV[i] is the position/length that denotes the i-th capture group within the XQuery regular expression match that is denoted by MV[0]. If the i-th parenthesized subexpression of PAT is not matched, then the position of MV[i] is 0 (zero).
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2 The position of MV[0] is never 0 (zero), since an XQuery regular expression match to PAT can never be no substring. An example of a capture group that is not matched occurs when S is a and PAT is (a)|(b). In this example, the match vector is given by MV[0] = (1,1), MV[1] = (1,1), and MV[2] = (0,0), since the second parenthesized subexpression has no match.
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
The result of this Subclause is a list LOMV of match vectors, defined as follows:
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
Let P0 be SP − 1 (one), and let L0 be 0 (zero).
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2 WG3:SQL-045 = DM32.2-2011-00___ WG3:UTC-013 P02-NLD-008
For i 1 (one), Pi and Li are defined recursively as follows. Let Pi be the position in units U of the first XQuery regular expression match of PAT in S such that Pi > Pi−1 + Li−1 − 1 and Pi > Pi−1, and let Li be the length in units U of this match.
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2 The sequence Pi is strictly increasing and bounded above by LEN + 1 (one), so this recursive definition terminates after finding a finite number of disjoint matches.
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
Let N be the number of XQuery regular expression matches found.
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2 It is possible that there are no matches, in which case N is 0 (zero), and LOMV is empty. (P0, L0) = (SP − 1, 0) is not included in the result; it is merely used as the position to start seeking the first match.
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
For i between 1 (one) and N, let MVi be the match vector such that:
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
MVi[0] is the position/length whose position is Pi and whose length is Li.
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
For j between 1 (one) and G, MVi[j] is the position/length
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
Case:
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
If the j-th parenthesized subexpression of PAT is not matched in the i-th XQuery regular expression match, then position 0 (zero) and length 0 (zero).
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
Otherwise, the position and length of the j-th capture group within the i-th XQuery regular expression match.
WG3:WLG-027 = H2-2005-292R2
Let LOMV be the list of N match vectors MVi in order from 1 (one) to N.

If FUNCTION is specified, then the SQL-invoked routine that is identified shall be an SQL-invoked regular function. If PROCEDURE is specified, then the SQL-invoked routine that is identified shall be an SQL-invoked procedure. If STATIC METHOD is specified, then the SQL-invoked routine that is identified shall be a static SQL-invoked method. If CONSTRUCTOR METHOD is specified, then the SQL-invoked routine that is identified shall be an SQL-invoked constructor method. If INSTANCE METHOD is specified or implicit, then the SQL-invoked routine that is identified shall be an instance SQL-invoked method. If ROUTINE is specified, then the SQL-invoked routine that is identified is either an SQL-invoked function or an SQL-invoked procedure.

WG3:KMG-033 = DM32.2-2010-00090 WG3:USN-024, P02-JPN-064 This ensures that the updatable columns of SUPERT can be determined when the view is created and will not be subject to change as a result of adding the subview. It also ensures that UPDATE column privileges on SUPERT can be established solely by examining the original of SUPERT, and need not change as the result of adding a subview. In more detail, the rule says that if a column of a referenceable view RV is a column reference to a column of the basis table of RV, then in every subview SUBRV, that column must be a column reference to the corresponding column in the basis table of SUBRV.

The character string value returned in an SQLSTATE parameter comprises a 2-character class code followed by a 3-character subclass code, each with an character set that has a one-octet character encoding form and is restricted to s and s. , specifies the class code for each condition and the subclass code or codes for each class code.
Ottawa decisions DBL:CWB-161/X3H2-98-214 DBL:LGW-049R2/X3H2-97-222 FCD1/1998 GBR-P02-354 KAW-058/X3H2-91-256 USA#83 WG3:FAO-021R1 = H2-2008-___ CD1 2009, WG3:CJU-015 JPN-P02-169, 2009-08-14 WG3:PEK-022 = DM32.2-2014-00___ WG3:UTC-013 P02-ISO-013
Class codes that begin with one of the s 0, 1, 2, 3, or 4 or one of the s A, B, C, D, E, F, G, or H are returned only for conditions defined in the ISO/IEC 9075 series or in any other International Standard. The range of such class codes is called standard-defined classes. Some such class codes are reserved for use by specific International Standards, as specified elsewhere in this Clause. Subclass codes associated with such classes that also begin with one of those 13 characters are returned only for conditions defined in the ISO/IEC 9075 series or some other International Standard. The range of such subclass codes is called standard-defined subclasses. Subclass codes associated with such classes that begin with one of the s 5, 6, 7, 8, or 9 or one of the s I, J, K, L, M, N, O, P, Q, R, S, T, U, V, W, X, Y, or Z are reserved for conditions and are called subclasses.

All subclass codes except 000, which means no subclass, associated with such classes are reserved for conditions and are called subclasses. The ISO/IEC 9075 series reserves SQLSTATE class HZ for Remote Database Access errors, which may occur when an SQL-client interacts with an SQL-server across a communications network using an RDA Application Context. defines a number of exception conditions that shall be detected in a conforming ISO RDA implementation.
If an SQL-implementation using RDA reports a condition shown in , for a given exception condition, then it shall use the SQLSTATE class code HZ and the subclass codes shown, and shall set the values of CLASS_ORIGIN to ISO 9075 and SUBCLASS_ORIGIN as indicated in , when those exceptions are retrieved by a .
An SQL-implementation using client-server communications other than RDA may report conditions corresponding to the conditions shown in , using the SQLSTATE class code HZ and the corresponding subclass codes shown. It may set the values of CLASS_ORIGIN to ISO 9075 and SUBCLASS_ORIGIN as indicated in . Any other communications error shall be returned with a subclass code from the range, with CLASS_ORIGIN set to ISO 9075 and SUBCLASS_ORIGIN set to an character string.

WG3:W12-024 SQL optional feature taxonomy
********************************************************************* Features of the SQL standard are defined by their "code"s. Each feature has a unique code that comprises a single ASCII letter followed by three ASCII digits. The initial letter feature codes indicates the provenance of the features: A -- Features defined in SQL/MDA B -- Features related to host language bindings, including embedded SQL, dynamic SQL, module language, direct invocation, and SQL-invoked routine language C -- Features defined in SQL/CLI E -- Features that were defined in the Entry level of SQL-92 F -- Features that were defined by FIPS 127-2 (FIPS is an acronym for Federal Information Processing Standard) G -- Features defined in SQL/PGQ and GQL J -- Features defined in SQL/OLB and SQL/JRT (Java-related parts) M -- Features defined in SQL/MED N -- Features defined in SQL/Stream P -- Features defined in SQL/PSM R -- Features related to row pattern matching S -- Features related to user-defined types and collection types T -- Features that were defined in SQL:1999 ("SQL3"), plus JSON features X -- Features defined in SQL/XML *********************************************************************

In , Feature ID values containing a hyphen and additional digits indicate subfeatures that help to define complete features, which are in turn indicated by Feature ID values without a hyphen. The set of subfeatures of a feature is intended to itemize noteworthy special cases of the feature without necessarily being exhaustive of the feature. In addition, subfeatures of a feature are not necessarily mutually exclusive; in some cases, one subfeature may subsume another subfeature.

— — Routine is the collective term for functions, methods, and procedures. This feature requires a conforming SQL-implementation to support both user-defined functions and user-defined procedures. An SQL-implementation that conforms to Core SQL will support at least one language for writing routines; that language can be SQL. If the language is SQL, then the basic specification capability in Core SQL is the ability to specify a one-statement routine. Support for overloaded functions and procedures is not part of Core SQL.
